title: The difficulty: how can premotion consist with created freedom?
source_text: XIII. Cum vero juxta eorum sententiam, divina ista praemotio locum habeat non minus in agentibus liberis quam in necessariis, inde oritur non parva difficultas, quomodo illud cum creaturarum libertate constare possit. Si enim Voluntas nostra nihil agere potest, nisi a Deo prius moveatur, atque ad opus applicetur, quomodo censeri poterit domina sui actus, & indifferens esse ad agendum, vel non agendum; quandoquidem non habet in sua potestate divinam illam motionem & applicationem, quae ad singulos ejus actus praerequiritur? Et rursus quum Deus Voluntatem movet & applicat ad opus, qui possit dici Voluntas libere operari, cum non possit non operari, & motioni divinae resistere?
pass_a_gloss: But since according to their opinion, that divine premotion has place no less in free agents than in necessary ones, thence arises no small difficulty, how that can consist with the liberty of creatures. For if our Will can do nothing, unless it be first moved by God, and applied to the work, how can it be thought the mistress of its act, and to be indifferent to acting, or not acting; since it does not have in its power that divine motion and application, which is prerequired to each of its acts? And again when God moves the Will and applies it to the work, how can the Will be said to operate freely, since it cannot not operate, and resist the divine motion?
pass_b_english: Since on their view this divine premotion applies to free agents no less than to necessary ones, a considerable difficulty arises: how can it be reconciled with the freedom of creatures?

If our will can do nothing unless God first moves it and applies it to its work, how can it be considered mistress of its own act and indifferent to acting or not acting, when the divine motion and application required beforehand for each of its acts is not in its power? And again, when God moves the will and applies it to its work, how can the will be said to act freely, when it can neither refrain from acting nor resist the divine motion?

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
